Empirical Research Plan: “Did World War II and the G.I. Bill raise the schooling of returning veterans?”

================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Method:  Fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity-in-Time (FRD) combined with Two-Stage Least Squares.

Rationale  
• Veteran status (and hence GI-Bill eligibility) jumps sharply—but not perfectly—at a clearly defined birth-date cutoff that determined draft eligibility for WWII.  
• Men born on or before 30 June 1927 were ≥18 before the war ended (2 Sept 1945) and were draft-eligible; those born later were not.  
• This creates a strong discontinuous increase in the probability of being a veteran, which we exploit as an instrument for actual veteran status.  
• Because some men on the “eligible” side still did not serve (medical deferments, etc.) and a few on the “ineligible” side volunteered, the design is fuzzy, so we estimate the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) of veteran status on schooling.

An RD-in-time design (rather than DID) avoids pooling heterogeneous pre/post cohorts and requires weaker parallel-trends assumptions.

================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
• Running variable:  Birth date (in quarters, qBirth = year + quarter/4).  
• Cutoff (c):  qBirth = 1927 Q2. Anyone born ≤ c was draft-eligible.

• First-stage (treatment) variable:  Veteranᵢ  = 1 if individual i reports WWII service.  
• Instrument (Zᵢ):  Eligibleᵢ  = 1{qBirthᵢ ≤ c}.  

• Control group:  Men born just after the cutoff (e.g., 1927 Q3–1930 Q4); they were too young to be drafted and thus rarely served in WWII, yet are close in age, facing similar macro conditions.  

• Treated compliers:  Men induced into service by falling on the eligible side of the cutoff.

Sample:  White and Black U.S.-born males observed in the 1960 & 1970 Public-Use 1% Census samples whose qBirth ∈ [1920Q1, 1935Q4] (±8 years around cutoff).

================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at cutoff  
 Conditional on a smooth function of birth date, expected schooling in absence of treatment is continuous at 1927 Q2. Plausible because nothing else changed discretely on that date that would directly affect later education.

A2. No precise manipulation of birth date  
 Parents in the 1920s could not time births to avoid a yet-unknown future war draft; measurement error in reported birth date is minimal in Census data.

A3. First-stage relevance (discontinuity in service)  
 Historical records show veteran rates jump by ~40 p.p. at the cutoff—easily testable.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA)  
 One man’s service doesn’t change another man’s schooling near the cutoff in ways that violate SUTVA; reasonable at individual level.

A5. Local polynomial specification captures smooth trends  
 Choosing bandwidths via honest MSE minimizes bias from functional-form misspecification.

================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Other policies correlated with birth cohort (Korean GI Bill, changing compulsory schooling laws)  
 • Remedy: Limit bandwidth to ±6–8 birth cohorts; include state-of-birth fixed effects and state-level controls (e.g., compulsory schooling age in 1930).  
 • Show placebo RD at other fake cutoffs.

T2. Differential mortality by veteran status (only survivors appear in 1960/70)  
 • Remedy: Show RD in 1950 Census survival rates (micro-data samples exist) or use life-table adjustments; argue any selective mortality would bias downward (vets more likely to die), making estimates conservative.

T3. Measurement error in veteran status or birth date  
 • Remedy: Verify reporting consistency across the two Census waves; restrict to individuals with birth quarter imputed directly (not age-heaped); show that first-stage remains strong.

================================================================
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------------ 0. Packages -----------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast OLS & IV
library(rdrobust)    # RD estimates
library(modelsummary)

# ------------------ 1. Load Data ----------------
c60 <- read_csv("census1960.csv")
c70 <- read_csv("census1970.csv")
census <- bind_rows(c60, c70) %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(substr(file, 7, 10)))   # keep track of wave

# ------------------ 2. Variable Construction ----
analysis <- census %>%
  filter(sex == "male", warservice %in% c("WWII","None")) %>%   # drop Korea/Vietnam
  mutate(
    qBirth = birth_year + (birth_quarter - 1)/4,
    cutoff = 1927 + 1/2,                     # 1927Q2
    elig   = if_else(qBirth <= cutoff, 1, 0),
    veteran = if_else(warservice == "WWII", 1, 0),
    educ_yrs = case_when(
        educ == "No schooling"              ~ 0,
        educ == "1st-4th grade"             ~ 3,
        educ == "5th-8th grade"             ~ 6,
        educ == "Some high school"          ~ 10,
        educ == "High school graduate"      ~ 12,
        educ == "Some college"              ~ 14,
        educ == "College graduate"          ~ 16,
        educ == "Postgraduate"              ~ 18,
        TRUE ~ NA_real_),
    black = race == "black",
    statebirth = factor(state_birth)
  ) %>%
  filter(qBirth >= 1920 & qBirth <= 1935)          # bandwidth +/-8 yrs

# ------------------ 3. First-Stage Check --------
rd_first <- rdrobust(y = analysis$veteran,
                     x = analysis$qBirth - analysis$cutoff,
                     c = 0)
summary(rd_first)

# ------------------ 4. 2SLS Main Specification --
# Local linear within h bandwidth chosen by rdrobust
h <- rd_first$bws[1]

main <- analysis %>%
  filter(abs(qBirth - cutoff) <= h)

iv_res <- feols(educ_yrs ~ 1 | veteran ~ elig,
                data = main,
                cluster = ~statebirth)
etable(iv_res, dict = c("veteran" = "WWII Veteran",
                        "educ_yrs" = "Years of Schooling"))

# ------------------ 5. Robustness: Alt Bandwidth -
for(h_alt in c(2,4,6)){                # ±2,4,6 yrs
  tmp <- analysis %>% filter(abs(qBirth - cutoff) <= h_alt)
  cat("\nBandwidth:", h_alt, "years\n")
  print( feols(educ_yrs ~ 1 | veteran ~ elig,
               data = tmp, cluster = ~statebirth) )
}

# Placebo cutoff at 1925Q2
placebo <- analysis %>% mutate(elig_pl = (qBirth <= 1925.5))
feols(educ_yrs ~ 1 | veteran ~ elig_pl,
      data = placebo, cluster = ~statebirth)
```

================================================================
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Theory: The GI Bill paid full tuition plus a stipend; college costs were low, returns to college high. I expect an increase of roughly 1.2–1.5 years of schooling for compliers at the cutoff (≈ 30–40 percentage-point rise in college completion probability).

================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RD)
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Large first-stage (relevance) …………………… 1  
C2: No precise manipulation of running variable … 1  
C3: Continuity of potential outcomes ……………… 0.8  
C4: Correct functional form / bandwidth ………… 0.8  
C5: No spillovers / SUTVA ………………………… 0.9  

Overall internal validity ≈ 4.5 / 5.

================================================================
This plan delivers a transparent, well-powered estimate of the causal effect of WWII service—and, by extension, GI-Bill eligibility—on veterans’ educational attainment.
